Prigov’s “New Anthropology,” similar to the monsters it conjures, transcends fixed categories and calls for a rethinking of the boundaries that structure human thought, culture, and power. 1 ARTICLE IN PRESS Introduction Dmitry Aleksandrovich Prigov (1940–2007) was a prominent Russian dissident artist and one of the initiators of Moscow Conceptualism. Despite initial rejection from mainstream Soviet media due to the satirical nature of his work, Prigov became a central figure in the underground literature, known as samizdat. Proficient in both poetry and visual arts, he embodied the “synthesising artist” ideal championed by the “Silver Age” philosophers (Zorin, 2010, p. 447). Prigov’s poetry was pivotal in Russia’s avant-garde scene, skilfully deconstructing Socialist Realism and critiquing the prevailing discourse on official Soviet culture. Boris Groys lauded Prigov as the artist “who completed the revolution of Russian poetry” (2010, pp. 407–408), and “the first writer to take a radical post-utopian position” (199S2, p. 95). Prigov’s works of art S have also gained international acclaim and are featured in prestigious museum collections, E including the Hermitage Museum in Russia, MuseumR Ludwig in Germany, Centre Georges P Pompidou in France, and the Tate Modern in the United Kingdom. N Moscow Conceptualism represents a revolutionary approach to visual communication and I literary creation within the framework of Soviet postmodernism. It challenges grand narratives E L and encourages open-ended interpretations. Prigov (2019) described Conceptualism as a C “mirror” for Russian culture, aIllowing it to see itself for the first time (p. 253). Reflecting on T Russian society througRh Conceptualism, Prigov’s work stands out for its strong political A consciousness, particularly when examining the late Soviet and post-Soviet eras. A key theme in his creative output is the “New Anthropology” (Novaya Antropologiya), a uniquely Russian exploration of the question of humanity. While engaging with the decentring of the human, as observed in Western anthropology, Prigov imbued the concept with a distinctly Moscow Conceptualist sensibility, prioritising spirituality and artistic expression over theoretical or scientific frameworks. He envisioned a new form of existence, depicting the “new homo sapiens” as a “floundering monster, divided internally into human and non-human parts” (Golynko-Volfson, 2007, pp. 271–272). Over three decades, Prigov wrote more than 100 poems and created nearly 100 portraits of these monstrous beings, reflecting his insights into the spirituality of contemporary society. Literary critic Irina Prokhorova (2017) even referred to Prigov as “Russia’s Dante of the 20th century” (p. i). 2 ARTICLE IN PRESS Prigov’s portrayal of monsters has sparked scholarly discussions in both Russian and international academia, but much of the focus has been on specific genres. Monsters in image: Prigov’s Bestiary as a multicultural symbolic system Prigov first brought his initial conception of the “new homo sapiens” to life in his paintings, beginning in the 1970s with his Bestiary (Bestiarij) graphic series, which depict monstrous creatures. The medieval bestiary, or “book of beasts,” served as an important source of inspiration for Prigov. Typically, bestiaries compiled descriptions of real and mythical animals, each accompanied by an etymological explanation connecting the creature’s name to its behaviour (Verner, 2005, p. 95). Echoing this medieval form, Prigov’s Bestiary comprises more than one hundred differently shaped monsters, forming a strikinSgly distinctive portrait gallery. S In medieval times, bestiaries served as resources for sermons and monastic teachings, E combining words and images to fix doctrinal mysterRies and moral precepts in the memory P (Clark & McMunn, 1989, p. 3; Rowland, 1989, p. 21). In contrast, Prigov’s Bestiary, with its N deliberately ambiguous monsters, emerged during the Soviet Union’s “Stagnation” (Zastoj) I period. Rather than upholding the reinforcing of official narratives, it subtly questioned and E L challenged them. Unable to be publicly displayed due to censorship, these works became part C of the underground art scene. ISome of these creatures were originally displayed on the walls T of Prigov’s Moscow apRartment, then later recreated in photographs at the Belyaevo Gallery A near his former home (Fig. 1). As Fig. 1 illustrates, each piece in this series demonstrates strong internal and external cohesion, with consistent proportions, materials and techniques. This aesthetic aligns Bestiary with the stylistic principles of Western Pop Art, which began to influence unofficial Soviet art in the 1960s. Moscow conceptualists often juxtaposed Western consumer culture with the ideological saturation of Soviet propaganda, underscoring what Elisabeth Sussman (1990) describes as the “redundancy and overabundance of ideological propagandistic graphic production” (p. 64). As Prigov (2019) observed: “A certain parallel to American Pop Art emerged in the Soviet Union during this period (albeit with some expected time lags). These similarities can be exclusively attributed to the underlying principles and essence of art construction” (p. 523). While Prigov’s Bestiary adopts methods akin to Pop Art’s structured 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS processes and mass reproduction, it departs from Andy Warhol’s iconic repetition of singular images, such as his Marilyn Monroe series. Instead, Prigov’s monsters embody multiplicity and hybridity within a unified framework. The fantastical creatures in Bestiary exhibit a unique blend of various animal traits: elephant trunks, rhinoceros horns, horse sideburns, camel humps, bird wings, and scorpion tails. Interwoven with these animalistic traits are distinctly human elements, including human eyes, five-fingered hands, and sexual organs. Most monsters are depicted naked, with graphic representations of breasts and genitals. In contrast, C the hermaphroditic body is frIequently regarded as monstrous due to its inherent ambiguity. JSON: Name: prigov_new_anthropology_multimodal Title: Multimodal computational analysis of Dmitry Prigov's "New Anthropology": testing integrated symbolic systems across poetry and Bestiary images Short Hypothesis: If Prigov's "New Anthropology" constitutes an integrated multimodal symbolic system, then specific symbolic motifs (e.g., left eye, cups, alchemical triangles, numeric indices, named initials) will co-occur across his poems and Bestiary images at rates significantly greater than in matched control corpora, and a classifier trained on motif labels from one modality will predict corresponding motif labels in the other modality with accuracy significantly above chance (p < 0.01). Related Work: Prior scholarship on Prigov has produced detailed qualitative readings of his poetic and visual motifs and placed his work in Moscow Conceptualism and posthumanist debates; separate streams of work analyse his poems or his Bestiary images individually. In digital humanities and computer vision, multimodal representation learning and vision-language models enable cross-modal retrieval and symbol alignment but have mainly been applied to contemporary, well-annotated corpora and mainstream languages; symbolic motif detection in historical artworks remains underdeveloped. Existing computational approaches typically rely on either unimodal text-topic models or image feature clustering, lack focused symbol lexica for artist-specific iconography, and produce limited statistical tests of cross-modal integration. Limitations include (1) qualitative-only interpretations with limited reproducibility; (2) absence of a purpose-built Prigov multimodal dataset; (3) small-sample risk and annotation bottlenecks for historic artworks; and (4) inadequate baselines for testing whether motif co-occurrence exceeds chance or is distinctive to an artist versus a period. Abstract: This project operationalizes Dmitry Prigov’s concept of a "New Anthropology" by testing whether his poetic and visual outputs form an empirically integrated multimodal symbolic system. We assemble a linked corpus comprising Prigov’s monster poems and Bestiary portraits, annotate a focused lexicon of recurring motifs (ocular motif, cups, triangles, numeric indices, initials, color tokens), and apply a pipeline combining symbolic annotation, statistical co-occurrence testing, and multimodal representation learning. Main contributions are: (1) a reproducible multimodal dataset for Prigov studies; (2) statistically rigorous tests of motif co-occurrence against matched control corpora; and (3) cross-modal classifiers and retrieval models that evaluate whether motifs learned in one modality generalize to the other. Expected outcomes are measurable evidence for or against an integrated symbolic practice in Prigov’s work and a methodological template for quantitative inter-art research that links historic visual and textual iconographies. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Prigov corpus: 119 monster-themed poems and 100 Bestiary images (high-resolution scans), metadata (title, date, provenance, documented initials). (B) Supplementary Prigov texts/images: up to 250 additional textual items and 50 visual works for robustness checks. (C) Control corpora: 200 poems and 200 images from contemporaneous Moscow conceptualists and 200 images from Soviet official visual culture matched by period and resolution. Annotation: create a motif lexicon of 12 discrete motif labels (left_eye, cup_black, cup_red, triangle_up, triangle_down, broken_egg, initials_circle, red_blood_tear, world_tree_branch, chakras_wheel, omniscient_eye_text, numeric_index_117). Two annotators label all images and poem passages; compute Cohen's kappa; accept labels with kappa >= 0.7. Preprocessing: OCR text with Russian model, tokenize and lemmatize; images resized to 224x224, color-normalized. Baselines: (1) unimodal text topic model (LDA) motif association; (2) image-only CNN clustering (ResNet50 features + k-means) motif frequencies; (3) random-permutation baseline (motif labels shuffled across items); (4) zero-shot CLIP retrieval (multilingual CLIP). Core models: (A) supervised symbol detector (Mask R-CNN fine-tuned on annotated symbols) for image motifs; (B) ruBERT embeddings fine-tuned to predict motif labels from poem segments; (C) cross-modal embedding via CLIP fine-tuned on paired poem-image items; (D) supervised cross-modal classifier: train on text motif labels to predict image motif labels and vice versa (logistic regression and feedforward network on top of embeddings). Evaluation metrics: motif co-occurrence significance (chi-square, pointwise mutual information), classifier accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, mean average precision (mAP) for retrieval, clustering purity, and permutation p-values (10,000 permutations). Experimental protocol: 5-fold cross-validation for all classifiers; report mean and 95% CI. Ablation studies: (1) remove color channels from images to evaluate color-token contribution; (2) train models using only annotated symbolic labels versus only learned features; (3) train cross-modal classifier on Prigov corpus and test on control corpus and vice versa. Comparison studies: compare motif co-occurrence rates and classifier cross-modal transfer accuracy between Prigov corpus and control corpora; test whether classifier trained on Prigov data predicts motifs in control corpus no better than chance. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: OCR errors on historical Russian orthography and idiosyncratic typography may corrupt textual inputs and reduce embedding quality; small dataset size (≈100–250 items per modality) risks overfitting when fine-tuning large models; iconographic variability and stylization in hand-drawn Bestiary images may limit detector performance. Annotation biases: cultural interpretive variance may reduce label reliability despite inter-annotator agreement thresholds; curated motif lexicon may omit latent symbols. Statistical limitations: limited sample sizes constrain statistical power for detecting small effect sizes and generalization beyond Prigov to other artists or periods. Model limitations: pretrained multilingual CLIP or ruBERT may underperform on poetic language and historic pictorial conventions, producing poor cross-modal alignment. Data governance: copyright or museum access restrictions may limit dataset release or replication. Scalability: fine-tuning vision-language models and Mask R-CNN requires GPU resources; larger-scale replication may be compute-intensive. Interpretive limits: computational detection of motif co-occurrence does not by itself establish intended semantic meaning or authorial intent and may conflate stylistic coincidence with conceptual integration.
